fatal_errors: The alloy is incorrectly assumed to be nearly single-phase and nanocrystalline with abundant high-angle grain boundaries; the target material is an as-cast, solidification-segregated dual-BCC alloy with W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions.

The proposed 800–1100 °C regime lies outside the reported room-temperature-to-500 °C mechanical-testing boundary and cannot reconstruct the observed transition in indentation cracking between 200 and 400 °C.
The mechanism assigns ductility to grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recovery without evidence that either process occurred in the target alloy.

The controlled comparison does not isolate lattice distortion or grain-boundary effects because composition, phase constitution, segregation, grain structure, and processing route all differ simultaneously.

The pure-tungsten baseline is materially inaccurate at elevated temperature: the reported tungsten becomes ductile near 400 °C rather than retaining minimal plasticity throughout high-temperature loading.
The cited evidence concerns different alloy chemistries, processing states, irradiation conditions, or room-temperature tests and does not validate the proposed mechanism in as-cast WTaTiVZr.
explanation: The response captures only the broad directional claim that WTaTiVZr may outperform pure tungsten in ductility and toughness. It does not reconstruct the actual material state, test window, baseline behavior, or proposed compositional and microstructural interpretation. In particular, it replaces the observed segregated dual-BCC dendritic structure with an unsupported nanocrystalline single-phase structure and moves testing to 800–1100 °C, whereas the relevant evidence spans room temperature to 500 °C. Its experiment can compare overall performance but cannot attribute any difference specifically to lattice distortion, grain-boundary sliding, or dynamic recovery. A discriminating test would require matched grain size and processing state, direct characterization of the dual-phase segregation, and deformation measurements within the reported temperature range, especially across the disappearance of HEA indentation cracks above 200 °C.
